An identity expressing expected weak satisfaction as one minus the average weak-failure probability then yields the robustness lower bound. Finally, since the loss is a fixed constant times the square-root function, it is Big-O of the square root of epsilon by reflexivity and closure under left multiplication by a constant. Combining the robustness statement with this asymptotic estimate provides the required algorithm and loss function.
nl_theorem: Consider Boolean promise templates given by finitely many relation pairs, each consisting of a strong relation contained in a weak relation of the same positive arity, with a common upper bound on arities. For such a template, one models finite promise-CSP instances (variables and constraints), Boolean assignments, the fractions of constraints strongly or weakly satisfied, approximate strong satisfiability, and uniform randomized algorithms that output a probability distribution over assignments together with a running-time cost, along with the notions of polynomial running time, expected weak satisfaction, and robustness with a prescribed loss function. Say a template admits Majority if every odd-arity Boolean majority operation preserves each of its relation pairs. The theorem states: for any Boolean promise template that admits Majority, there exist a uniform randomized algorithm and a real loss function such that the algorithm runs in polynomial time, is robust with that loss (on every instance that is at least a one-minus-epsilon fraction strongly satisfiable, its expected weakly satisfied fraction is at least one minus the loss), and the loss is Big-O of the square root of epsilon as epsilon tends to zero through nonnegative values.

core_claim: Level complexity functions of line arrangements both bound above and force below the number of output changes of stationary divisor apportionment methods.

metainfo.paper: New Combinatorial Insights for Monotone Apportionment

nl_proof: The two conclusions are proved separately and combined. For the upper bound, one reduces any apportionment instance with n states to an auxiliary arrangement of at most 2n−1 lines together with a level index whose k-level complexity dominates the windowed complexity of the top level of the instance's associated arrangement; the number of breaking points is at most one more than this windowed complexity because every interior breaking point occurs at a top-level vertex and the level vertex set is finite. Splitting on whether the reduced line count exceeds the complexity-bound threshold, one uses either the uniform g-bound or the quadratic cardinality bound on level complexity, and then absorbs the residual constants and the additive one using the eventual two-scale domination of g, yielding a bound C·g(n). For the lower bound, one starts from the stable k-level witness for h, regularizes the possibly degenerate level so that half of its vertices become simple crossings of a single fixed strict-below rank with injective abscissa, models these crossings with positive rational line parameters via simultaneous rational approximation and a common integral multiplier, and finally realizes the rationally modeled crossings as genuine breaking points of an explicitly constructed apportionment instance through a projective normalization placing each crossing inside its divisor rounding intervals. This gives a positive constant times h(n) breaking points for each large n. Taking the conjunction of the two results establishes the theorem.
nl_theorem: Work with non-vertical lines in the plane recorded by slope and intercept, indexed line arrangements (finite sets of labeled lines), and the vertices of the k-level of such an arrangement (crossings of two distinct lines whose strict-below and on-level line counts bracket k), whose count is the k-level complexity. An apportionment instance consists of a positive number of states n, a positive population for each state, and a positive house size H; its stationary δ-divisor output is the set of nonnegative integer allocations summing to H that arise from some positive divisor under δ-rounding, and its breaking points are the terminal parameter 1 together with every δ in (0,1] where the output changes from the left. Let num_breaking_points denote the cardinality of the breaking-point set. Say g bounds the k-level complexity if some constant times g(m) uniformly bounds the k-level complexity of every m-line arrangement for all sufficiently large m and all levels k, and g additionally has eventual domination at the two-to-one scale. Say h witnesses a k-level lower bound if for all sufficiently large m there is an m-line arrangement and a level with complexity at least a fixed constant times h(m), together with stable perturbation data expressing each level vertex as a distinct simple crossing of one of two admissible strict-below ranks with injective abscissa. Then, whenever g bounds the k-level complexity and h witnesses a k-level lower bound, two things hold: (i) there is a positive constant C and a threshold N such that every apportionment instance with at least N states has at most C·g(n) breaking points; and (ii) there is a positive constant c and a threshold N' such that for every n at least N' there exists an apportionment instance with exactly n states having at least c·h(n) breaking points.

core_claim: On a path of least-squares predictors, the final predictor's mean squared error competes with any bounded-coefficient linear predictor up to a term proportional to the square root of total improvement.

metainfo.paper: Networked Information Aggregation via Machine Learning

nl_proof: Apply the MSE decomposition/competitive bound to the final predictor ŷ_b against the comparison predictor g, giving MSE(ŷ_b) ≤ MSE(g) + 2|⟪g, ŷ_b − y⟫| + 2|⟪ŷ_b, ŷ_b − y⟫|. The self-orthogonality clause of path-orthogonality at position b makes the last term zero. To bound the correlation term, expand g by linearity of the inner product and bound each |⟪x_l, ŷ_b − y⟫| by shifting the residual through the multiaccurate position m where l is observed, using Cauchy–Schwarz together with a distance estimate ‖ŷ_b − ŷ_m‖ ≤ √((b−a)ε). This distance estimate itself follows by telescoping the per-step MSE improvements (each equal to a squared predictor distance via the stability lemma), applying the triangle inequality along the path, squaring, and using a Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for sums of square roots plus the fact that the partial improvement on a terminal segment is at most the total ε. Summing the per-feature bounds with the ℓ¹-coefficient bound gives |⟪g, ŷ_b − y⟫| ≤ A_g·M_X·√((b−a)ε). Finally split √((b−a)ε) = √(b−a)·√ε and combine to obtain the stated inequality.
nl_theorem: Work in a real inner product space H (thought of as square-integrable random variables over a fixed distribution, with inner product the expected product and mean squared error MSE(f) = ‖f − y‖²). Let y be the target, x a family of feature vectors indexed by a type with decidable equality, S a function assigning to each path position a finite set of observed feature indices, and ŷ a family of predictions along the path that is path-orthogonal for (y, x, S): each ŷ_t is self-orthogonal (⟪ŷ_t, ŷ_t − y⟫ = 0), multiaccurate to its own features (⟪x_l, ŷ_t − y⟫ = 0 for l ∈ S_t), and multiaccurate to its successor's residual (⟪ŷ_t, ŷ_{t+1} − y⟫ = 0). Fix positions a < b, let F be the union of the feature sets over positions a+1,…,b, let α be real coefficients, and let g = Σ_{l∈F} α_l x_l. Assume the total improvement MSE(ŷ_a) − MSE(ŷ_b) = ε with ε ≥ 0, the coefficients satisfy Σ_{l∈F} |α_l| ≤ A_g, and each feature obeys ⟪x_l, x_l⟫ ≤ M_X² with M_X ≥ 0. Then MSE(ŷ_b) ≤ MSE(g) + 2·A_g·M_X·√(b−a)·√ε.

core_claim: For a fixed-horizon online minimization problem over an input alphabet with measurable singletons, if an (alpha, beta)-competitive algorithm exists for every finitely supported prior, then a single online algorithm achieves that guarantee against every input.

metainfo.paper: Online Algorithms via Minimax and Posterior Matching

nl_proof: The argument first establishes the conclusion on every finite set S of inputs and then globalizes it by compactness. Working with the space A of causal randomized online algorithms, one shows this space is compact: each factor of Borel probability measures on the compact action space is compact by Prokhorov's theorem, the product over all inputs is compact by Tychonoff's theorem, and the feasibility and causality constraints cut out a closed subset (feasibility being a full-mass constraint on a closed set, closed by upper semicontinuity via the portmanteau theorem, and causality being an equalizer of continuous pushforward maps under the continuous prefix projection). For a fixed finite set S, suppose for contradiction that no algorithm meets the bound everywhere on S. The affine evaluation map sending an algorithm nu to the vector (E_{nu_x}[cost] - alpha * OPT(x))_{x in S} has compact convex image (continuity of expected cost for weak convergence, plus the facts that mixtures of algorithms are algorithms and that expected cost is affine in mixtures). This image is disjoint from the closed convex box of vectors whose coordinates are all at most beta, so the geometric Hahn-Banach separation theorem yields a separating linear functional whose coefficients are shown to be nonpositive and not all zero; here measurability of singletons of the input alphabet is used so that the normalized coefficients define a genuine finitely supported prior as a finite combination of Dirac masses, against which integration reduces to a finite weighted sum. Applying the hypothesis to that prior contradicts the separation, proving the finite claim. Finally, for each input x the set C_x of algorithms meeting the bound at x is closed (preimage of a closed ray under a continuous map), every finite subfamily of the C_x has nonempty intersection with the compact space A by the finite-set result, and the finite intersection property for compact sets produces a common algorithm nu* satisfying the bound at every input.
nl_theorem: Fix a time horizon T (a natural number) and constants alpha, beta with alpha >= 0 and beta >= 0. Work with a measurable per-step input alphabet in which every singleton is a measurable set (i.e. the input alphabet has the measurable-singleton property), so that every finitely supported prior over inputs is a genuine finite combination of point masses and cost integrands are pointwise evaluated and summable; and with a compact metric space of per-step actions equipped with a distinguished base point (Borel, second-countable, metrizable, compact). Inputs are length-T sequences over the input alphabet and action sequences are length-T sequences over the action space. To each input x one assigns a compact set Y(x) of feasible action sequences, a cost function y -> cost(x, y) that is continuous, and an offline optimum OPT(x). A randomized online algorithm is a family nu = (nu_x) of Borel probability measures on the space of action sequences, indexed by inputs, that is (i) feasible, meaning nu_x gives mass 1 to the feasible set Y(x), and (ii) causal, meaning that whenever two inputs x, x' agree on their first t coordinates, the pushforwards of nu_x and nu_{x'} under the projection onto the first t actions coincide. A distribution D over inputs is finitely supported if the complement of some finite set is D-null. Suppose that for every finitely supported prior D over inputs there exists a randomized online algorithm nu^D whose expected cost satisfies E_{X ~ D} E_{Y ~ nu^D_X}[cost(X, Y)] <= alpha * E_{X ~ D}[OPT(X)] + beta. Then there exists a single randomized online algorithm nu* such that for every input x one has E_{Y ~ nu*_x}[cost(x, Y)] <= alpha * OPT(x) + beta.

core_claim: For a universally orthogonal calibration loss, the calibration error of a predictor under the true nuisance is at most half the nuisance-estimation error plus its calibration error under any nuisance estimate.

metainfo.paper: Orthogonal Causal Calibration (Extended Abstract)

nl_proof: Write v = g − g₀ and let ψ(t) be the conditional score at g₀ + t·v, so ψ(0) and ψ(1) are the conditional scores at g₀ and g. Using the existence hypothesis for the second directional derivatives at the shifted base points together with the translation identity g₀ + t·v + s·v = g₀ + (t+s)·v and the chain rule for one-dimensional restrictions, one shows that ψ is differentiable everywhere and that its derivative is differentiable everywhere, with ψ''(s) equal to the second nuisance derivative at g₀ + s·v in direction v. Universal orthogonality applied to g gives ψ'(0) = 0. If the nuisance-estimation error is infinite the right-hand side is infinite and the bound is immediate; otherwise let M be its finite nonnegative value. For s in [0,1] the point g₀ + s·v lies in the pointwise segment joining g and g₀ (constant weight s, using linearity of the injective evaluation map), and since the second directional derivative is even in its direction its norm there in direction g₀ − g equals its norm in direction v, so ‖ψ''(s)‖ is one term of the supremum defining the error and hence at most M. A second-order increment bound, obtained from the mean value inequality for right derivatives and a fencing argument against the boundary function (M/2)·t², yields ‖ψ(1) − ψ(0)‖ ≤ M/2, i.e. the conditional scores at g₀ and g differ by at most M/2 in norm. The contraction property for conditioning on the prediction transfers this to the calibration scores, and the triangle inequality gives ‖CalScore(θ, g₀)‖ ≤ M/2 + ‖CalScore(θ, g)‖. Passing to extended nonnegative reals and rewriting M/2 as one half of the nuisance-estimation error gives the claimed inequality.
nl_theorem: Consider an orthogonal calibration model with covariate, nuisance-index, and observation spaces, a real normed nuisance space G, a value space V, and a normed score space H. The model supplies a loss whose derivative in its first argument is a given function, an injective linear evaluation of nuisances as functions on the nuisance-index space, a conditional score defined as the conditional expectation given the covariate of the loss derivative evaluated at the prediction, and a calibration score defined as the conditional expectation of the conditional score given the prediction, with conditioning on the prediction contracting differences of conditional scores in norm. For a predictor θ and nuisance g, the calibration error Cal(θ, g) is the norm of the calibration score, and for nuisances g, h the nuisance-estimation error err(g, h; θ) is the supremum, over the pointwise segment joining g and h, of the norm of the second directional nuisance derivative of the conditional score in the repeated direction h − g. Let g₀ be the true nuisance. Assume the loss is universally orthogonal at g₀, meaning that for every predictor and every nuisance the directional derivative at g₀ of the conditional score along the line toward that nuisance vanishes, and assume all the relevant repeated second directional nuisance derivatives exist. Then for every nuisance g and every predictor θ, Cal(θ, g₀) ≤ (1/2) err(g, g₀; θ) + Cal(θ, g), the inequality being stated in the extended nonnegative reals.

core_claim: A deterministic online interval-prediction algorithm keeps every played interval nearly volume-optimal while bounding total coverage mistakes by a logarithmic factor times the miscoverage budget.

metainfo.paper: Online Conformal Prediction with Efficiency Guarantees

nl_proof: The volume bound is exactly the volume-guarantee field of the supplied meta-algorithm guarantee, so it is returned directly. For the mistake bound, one first establishes that any two intervals feasible on days beyond 2αT+1 must overlap on a common early day: since these late days have index above 2αT+1 > 0, feasibility is equivalent to making at most αT mistakes among the first 2αT+1 days, so each interval covers at least αT+1 of them; two subsets of a block of at most 2αT+1 days whose sizes sum to more than the block size must intersect (an inclusion–exclusion counting argument), yielding a shared covered day. This single-epoch condition is precisely the hypothesis required by the mistake-guarantee field, which then gives the total mistakes ≤ (2αT+1) + c_0·(log(1/minwidth)/log μ)·(αT+1). Finally, using αT ≥ 0, c_0 ≥ 0, and log(1/minwidth)/log μ ≥ 1, the additive (2αT+1) term is absorbed via the elementary inequality (2a+1) + C·L·(a+1) ≤ (C+2)·L·(a+1), producing the stated bound with constant c_0 + 2.
nl_theorem: Fix a scale lower bound minwidth > 0, a multiplicative volume approximation μ > 3, a target miscoverage rate α ≥ 0, a horizon T, and a sequence S = (y_0, …, y_{T-1}) of real points. Assume the scale is small enough that log(1/minwidth)/log μ ≥ 1. Suppose we are given the external meta-algorithm guarantee for these parameters, which supplies: the interval I_t played on each day t, a nonnegative constant c_0, the per-day volume bound vol(I_t) ≤ μ·max{Opt_S(α), minwidth}, and the conditional mistake bound stating that whenever all intervals feasible on any two days beyond 2αT+1 share a commonly covered day among the first 2αT+1 days (so those days form a single epoch), the total number of mistakes is at most (2αT+1) + c_0·(log(1/minwidth)/log μ)·(αT+1). Here Opt_S(α) is the smallest volume of a fixed interval achieving (1−α)-coverage in hindsight, feasibility on day t means the number of mistakes before t is at most R(t)·t with R(0)=1 and R(t)=αT/t otherwise, and a mistake occurs on day t when y_t is not covered by I_t. Then the played intervals satisfy vol(I_t) ≤ μ·max{Opt_S(α), minwidth} for every day t, and the total number of mistakes obeys the explicit bound (c_0 + 2)·(log(1/minwidth)/log μ)·(αT + 1).

core_claim: Any schedule whose step approximation minimizes the integration error against the information curve also minimizes the sampler's expected divergence error among all valid step schedules.

metainfo.paper: Optimal Inference Schedules for Masked Diffusion Models

nl_proof: Fix an arbitrary valid k-step schedule s. Apply the defining identity of the problem twice—once to s* and once to s—to rewrite both expected KL errors as the corresponding L1 integration errors between the information curve and its left Riemann step approximations. The minimality hypothesis on s* states precisely that the L1 error of s* is at most that of s, which after the rewriting yields eKL(s*) ≤ eKL(s).
nl_theorem: Consider a masked diffusion inference problem consisting of a finite token alphabet, a sequence length n, a data distribution over length-n sequences, an information curve Z (a real sequence with Z at index 1 equal to zero and monotone nondecreasing on the range 1 to n), and an expected KL error functional eKL on schedules. Assume the defining tie: for every k with 1 ≤ k ≤ n and every valid k-step schedule s for length n (each step at least 1 and the steps summing to n), eKL(s) equals the L1 integration error, over indices 1 to n, between Z and its k-step left Riemann step approximation induced by the node sequence N_a = 1 + sum of the first a−1 steps. Fix k with 1 ≤ k ≤ n and a valid k-step schedule s* whose induced left Riemann approximation minimizes this L1 error over all valid k-step schedules. Then s* minimizes the expected KL error: for every valid k-step schedule s, eKL(s*) ≤ eKL(s).

core_claim: Any online prediction algorithm facing the hard Bernoulli instance incurs expected multicalibration error growing at least on the order of the horizon to the two-thirds power.

metainfo.paper: Optimal Lower Bounds for Online Multicalibration

nl_proof: The bound is obtained by chaining two intermediate estimates. First, an anti-concentration argument shows there are a constant c₁ > 0 and a threshold T₁ such that for every hard instance with T ≥ T₁ the expected multicalibration error is at least c₁·√(mT); this proceeds by lower-bounding the expected multicalibration error by one third of the expected sum of the three group errors, and lower-bounding that sum by a fixed multiple of a spread–drift score built from far-round and near-round indicators. The spread–drift score is in turn bounded below by δ*·√(mT) using the trichotomy that each round is either far or near. Second, an elementary grid estimate gives a constant c₂ > 0 and a threshold T₂ such that √(mT) ≥ c₂·T^(2/3) whenever m ≥ 1 and m³ ≤ T < (m+1)³, using m ≥ T^(1/3)/2. Setting c = c₁·c₂ and T₀ = max(T₁, T₂) and combining the two inequalities yields E[MCerr_T(G)] ≥ c₁·√(mT) ≥ c₁·c₂·T^(2/3) = c·T^(2/3).
nl_theorem: Consider the online multicalibration hard instance, packaged as a probability space carrying: a horizon T and grid size m with 2 ≤ m and m³ ≤ T < (m+1)³; independent {0,1}-valued labels yᵗ whose means equal the round-robin hard contexts xᵗ = (⌈m/4⌉ + (t mod count))/m lying in [1/4, 3/4]; a sub-σ-algebra of algorithmic randomness independent of all labels; and [0,1]-valued predictions pᵗ that are online, i.e. measurable with respect to the algorithmic randomness joined with the σ-algebra of strictly earlier labels. With the fixed construction constant δ* = 1/100, threshold η = δ*·√(m/T), and hard group family g₀(x,v)=𝟙[v≥x+η], g₁(x,v)=𝟙[v≤x−η], g₂(x,v)=𝟙[|v−x|<η], define the expected multicalibration error as the integral over the space of maxᵢ Σ_{v∈V_T} |Σ_t 𝟙[pᵗ=v]·gᵢ(xᵗ,pᵗ)·(pᵗ−yᵗ)|. Then there exist a universal constant c > 0 and a threshold T₀ ∈ ℕ such that every such instance with T ≥ T₀ satisfies E[MCerr_T(G)] ≥ c·T^(2/3).

core_claim: For each downstream agent that best-responds to decision-calibrated predictions using the elimination algorithm, the constrained swap regret against the feasible benchmark is bounded by the calibration error.

metainfo.paper: Omniprediction with Long-Term Constraints

nl_proof: Fix an agent in N. It suffices to bound, for every map φ from the action space into the terminal feasible benchmark, the realized swap sum Σ_t (u(φ(a_t), y_t) − u(a_t, y_t)); the constrained swap regret is the finite supremum of these sums over all such maps, so a uniform bound transfers to it. For a fixed φ, decompose each round's term by inserting the two prediction-space quantities u(φ(a_t), p_t) and u(a_t, p_t), splitting the sum into three pieces. The first piece, the swapped prediction-minus-outcome gap, is controlled in absolute value by L·|A|·α₁(T/|A|): this follows by applying the calibration utility-error estimate to the auxiliary agent whose utility at a is the original utility at φ(a). That estimate itself first extends the Lipschitz bound from cube differences to arbitrary vectors v by writing v as ‖v‖_∞ times a difference of two cube points, giving |u(a,v)| ≤ L‖v‖_∞; then it rewrites the utility gap as Σ_a u(a, r_a) with r_a the calibration residual, bounds it by L·Σ_a ‖r_a‖_∞ ≤ L·Σ_a α₁(T(a)) using decision calibration, and applies Jensen's inequality for the concave α₁ with uniform weights together with Σ_a T(a) = T. The middle piece, Σ_t (u(φ(a_t), p_t) − u(a_t, p_t)), is nonpositive because the benchmark lies in every candidate set, so φ(a_t) is a candidate and a_t maximizes predicted utility over the candidate set. The third piece, the played action's prediction-minus-outcome gap, is bounded by L·|A|·α₁(T/|A|) by the same calibration utility-error estimate applied directly. Adding the three bounds yields 2·L·|A|·α₁(T/|A|). Since φ was arbitrary and the agent was arbitrary, the constrained swap regret bound holds for every agent in N.
nl_theorem: Let the action space be a finite nonempty type with decidable equality, and let the outcome coordinates form a finite nonempty type so that outcomes and predictions are vectors in the cube [0,1]^D. Fix natural numbers J and T and a constant L ≥ 0. Consider a set N of agents, each consisting of an action-indexed real-linear utility functional on R^D together with J real constraint functions. Fix common prediction and outcome sequences p, y : Fin T → [0,1]^D, and for every agent fix a sequence of maintained candidate action sets and a played-action sequence indexed by Fin T. Let α₁ : R → R be concave on R. Assume that every agent in N is L-admissible (each utility maps the cube into [0,1], each constraint maps the cube into [-1,1], and each utility is L-Lipschitz on the cube in the supremum norm), that each agent's candidate sets and played actions run the elimination algorithm relative to y and p (the played action always lies in and maximizes predicted utility over the current candidate set, and the terminal feasible benchmark is contained in every candidate set), that p is decision calibrated relative to y and the agent's played actions (for each action a, the supremum norm of the sum over rounds where a is played of p_t − y_t is at most α₁ of the number of such rounds), and that the terminal feasible benchmark A_{1:T}^c (actions satisfying every constraint at every round) is nonempty. Then every agent in N has constrained swap regret, the maximum over maps φ from actions into the benchmark of the total realized utility gain from replacing each played action a_t by φ(a_t), bounded by 2·L·|A|·α₁(T/|A|).

core_claim: A single deterministic algorithm family solves the online orthogonal vectors problem for every admissible parameter triple while meeting explicit query time, encoded space, and preprocessing time bounds.

metainfo.paper: Online Orthogonal Vectors Revisited

nl_proof: For each dimension pair we first fix an arbitrary fallback algorithm to serve at inadmissible parameter triples. For each triple, if the admissibility conditions 1 ≤ n, 1 ≤ i, and i ≤ d hold we select an algorithm meeting all three bounds, obtained by strong induction on i (uniformly in n and d): the case n = 1 stores the single input vector; the case i = 1 stores a complete answer table over all queries; and otherwise, using rounded recursive parameters n' = ⌈n^(1−1/i)⌉ and d' = d − d/i together with a pseudorandom partition of the database, correctness is transferred from a recursively obtained data structure for (n', d', i−1), while the query, space, and preprocessing bounds are closed by dedicated recurrence estimates and a database-versus-answer-table space dichotomy. At inadmissible triples we return the fallback algorithm, for which the admissibility implication is vacuous. Dependent choice packages these pointwise selections into a single family, and at every admissible triple the selected member satisfies exactly the required bounded-data-structure assertion.
nl_theorem: Consider Boolean vectors indexed by finitely many coordinates, where two such vectors are orthogonal exactly when the sum over all coordinates of the products of their bit values (viewed as natural numbers) is zero. A cost-accounted deterministic online orthogonal-vectors algorithm on n vectors of dimension d comprises a state type with an injective Boolean-list encoding, a preprocessing step that maps a database of n vectors to a state together with a charged running time, and a query step that maps a state and a query vector to a Boolean answer together with a charged running time; such an algorithm solves the problem when its answer is true precisely when some database vector is orthogonal to the query. Writing the partial binomial sum as the sum of binomial coefficients of d up to a given index, the theorem asserts the existence of a family of such algorithms indexed by natural numbers n, d, and i, so that for all n, d, i with 1 ≤ n, 1 ≤ i, and i ≤ d, the member indexed by that triple solves the online orthogonal-vectors problem, every query execution has charged time at most 2·i·d·n^(1−1/i), every preprocessed state has injective encoding length at most (partial binomial sum of d up to d/i)·i·d·n^(1−1/i), and every preprocessing execution has charged time at most (partial binomial sum of d up to d/i)·i·d·n.

core_claim: For any loss obeying an approximate triangle inequality over a hypothesis class of finite diameter, the online dimension is at most four times the approximation constant times the entropy potential.

metainfo.paper: Online Realizable Regression and Applications for ReLU Networks

nl_proof: Fix an arbitrary scaled Littlestone tree T realizable by H; it suffices to bound its branch value by 4c times the entropy potential of H, since the online dimension is the supremum of these values over realizable trees. The core is a branch-level entropy-potential bound: there exists an infinite branch b of T along which the total sum of node gaps is at most 4c times the entropy potential of H. This branch is built greedily. The key one-step estimate combines two facts about any internal node u with version space U and children version spaces U_0, U_1. First, a cover-splitting lemma shows that for every epsilon below the gap at u divided by 2c, the covering numbers of the two children add to at most that of U; this uses the relaxed triangle inequality applied to the induced pseudo-metric to show no single center can be within epsilon of points of both children, so a minimal cover of U splits into disjoint covers of the children. Second, from this splitting one derives a potential drop: some child b has entropy potential at most that of U minus the gap divided by 4c, obtained by measuring the set of epsilon where the child's covering number is at most half that of U and integrating the resulting logarithmic decrease over an interval of length the gap divided by 2c. A matching lower bound shows the gap divided by 4c is itself at most the potential of U, since on the same interval the covering number of U is at least 2, making the truncated subtraction genuine and yielding the additive form: some child satisfies potential of that child plus gap over 4c at most potential of U. Iterating this additive drop selects successive child bits, defining the branch b and nodes whose potentials telescope: for every n the sum of the first n scaled gaps plus the potential at depth n is at most the potential at the root, which equals the entropy potential of H because the empty node's version space is H. Dropping the nonnegative remaining potential and passing to the supremum over n gives that the sum of the gaps divided by 4c along b is at most the entropy potential of H; multiplying through by 4c yields the branch bound. Finally, the infimum over branches is at most this branch's value, and taking the supremum over all realizable trees gives the claimed bound on the online dimension.
nl_theorem: Let X be an instance domain, Y a label space, and H a class of hypotheses from X to Y. Let a loss function on Y be a c-approximate pseudo-metric for some c at least 1, meaning it vanishes on equal arguments, is symmetric, and satisfies the relaxed triangle inequality that any pairwise loss is at most c times the sum of the two losses to a common third label. Equip H with the induced sup pseudo-metric, the pointwise supremum of the loss between two hypotheses, and assume H has finite diameter, so its pairwise pointwise losses are uniformly bounded. Define the covering number N(U, epsilon) of a subset U of H as the least cardinality of a finite subset of H whose members epsilon-cover U in this pseudo-metric, and define the entropy potential of U as the lower Lebesgue integral of the base-2 logarithm of N(U, epsilon) over epsilon ranging from 0 to the diameter of H. Let the online dimension of H be the supremum, over all scaled Littlestone trees realizable by H, of the infimum over infinite branches of the sum of the node gaps along the branch, where each node gap is the loss between the two edge labels leaving that node. Then the online dimension of H is at most 4c times the entropy potential of H.

core_claim: For a regular non-isometric transport map, the time schedule that minimizes the uniform spatial Lipschitz constant of the interpolating velocity field is given by an explicit closed-form expression, split into three regimes.

metainfo.paper: Optimal Scheduling of Dynamic Transport

nl_proof: First one reduces the transport hypotheses to scalar hypotheses on f and g. Using positive mass of mu on Omega and absolute continuity, Omega has positive Lebesgue measure, forcing its affine span to be the whole space, so Omega is a set of unique differentiability and the derivative map is continuous on it. A Rayleigh-quotient identity in the eigenbasis bounds each extremal eigenvalue difference between two points by the operator-norm difference of the derivatives, giving continuity of f and g; the finite min is at most the finite max so g <= f, positivity of eigenvalues gives g_* > -1, and non-isometry yields a point where f or g is nonzero. Thus Omega, f, g, f*, g_* satisfy the scalar transport conditions. The proof then splits into the same three regimes as the statement. In every regime one first computes the supremal speed factor M(x) on [0,1] in closed form using compactness (extrema are attained) and the monotonicity of y/(1+xy): in the transition regime M(x) = max{ f*/(1+x f*), -g_*/(1+x g_*) }, in the expanding regime M(x) = f*/(1+x f*), and in the contracting regime M(x) = -g_*/(1+x g_*). Substituting M into the ODE and applying the chain rule shows that log(1 + f* tau(t)) or log(1 + g_* tau(t)) has constant derivative +/- Z^{-1}; the mean value theorem together with the endpoint conditions tau(0)=0, tau(1)=1 integrates this to a linear-in-t logarithm. Exponentiating and dividing by the nonzero extremum gives the stated formula. In the transition regime an additional algebraic lemma (using an arithmetic-geometric-mean inequality) shows that the constant C = (1/(4(g_*+1)))(2 - f*/g_* - g_*/f*) exceeds 1, that C = H/R with H = (1/2)(1 - f*/g_*) and R = 2(g_*+1)/(1 - g_*/f*), and that t_0 = log H / log C lies in [0,1]; the intermediate value theorem locates the crossover point a where tau(a) equals the transition value, monotonicity selects the correct branch of M on either side, and matching the two logarithmic identities at a identifies a = t_0, Z^{-1} = log C, and yields both branch formulas. The three cases are exhaustive, which completes the proof.
nl_theorem: Let d be a positive integer and work in d-dimensional Euclidean space. Let Omega be a nonempty compact convex set, let T be a continuously differentiable map on Omega whose derivative at each point s has a complete orthonormal eigenbasis e_i(s) with strictly positive eigenvalues sigma_i(s), and let mu, nu be probability measures that are absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, are supported on Omega, and satisfy the pushforward relation T_# mu = nu; assume moreover that sigma_i(s) is not equal to 1 for at least one s and i (non-isometry). Define f(s) = max_i sigma_i(s) - 1 and g(s) = min_i sigma_i(s) - 1, and set f* = sup_{s in Omega} f(s) and g_* = inf_{s in Omega} g(s). Let tau : R -> R be a schedule that is continuously differentiable, nondecreasing, maps [0,1] into itself, satisfies tau(0)=0 and tau(1)=1, and solves the normalized velocity ODE: there exists Z > 0 such that for every t in (0,1) the derivative of tau at t equals Z^{-1} times the reciprocal of M(tau(t)), where M(x) = max{ sup_{s in Omega} |f(s)/(1+x f(s))|, sup_{s in Omega} |g(s)/(1+x g(s))| }. Let t_0 = log((1/2)(1 - f*/g_*)) / ( log((1/4)(2 - f*/g_* - g_*/f*)) - log(g_* + 1) ). Then: (1) if g_* < 0 < f*, the logarithmic denominator defining t_0 is nonzero, and t_0 lies in [0,1], then tau satisfies tau(t_0) = -(1/2)(1/f* + 1/g_*) together with, for all t in [0,1], the branch tau(t) = (1/f*){ (1/(4(g_*+1)))(2 - f*/g_* - g_*/f*) }^t - 1/f* whenever t <= t_0 and the branch tau(t) = (1/2)(1/g_* - 1/f*){ 2(g_*+1)/(1 - g_*/f*) }^t { (1/2)(1 - f*/g_*) }^{1-t} - 1/g_* whenever t_0 <= t; (2) otherwise, if f* >= -g_*, then tau(t) = ((f*+1)^t - 1)/f* for all t in [0,1]; (3) otherwise (f* < -g_*), then tau(t) = ((g_*+1)^t - 1)/g_* for all t in [0,1].

core_claim: Coordinate-wise AdaGrad on smooth nonconvex objectives, with fixed problem data and growing horizon, drives its expected time-averaged gradient stationarity to zero at the explicit five-term asymptotic rate of the paper.

metainfo.paper: Provable Complexity Improvement of AdaGrad over SGD: Upper and Lower Bounds in Stochastic Non-Convex Optimization

nl_proof: Fix the universal constant furnished by the summed root-gradient estimate, which bounds the coordinate sum of expected roots of accumulated squared gradient coordinates by an explicit expression in the gradient budget (gap plus a step-size- and norm-weighted logarithmic budget), obtained by a Cauchy–Schwarz pairing of decorrelated and auxiliary step sizes, a Jensen-type square-root estimate with a subadditive denominator split and a second-moment noise bound, resolution of a quadratic inequality, a finite Cauchy–Schwarz over coordinates, and a radical split converting a root-of-two-times-horizon factor into a fourth-root-of-horizon factor. Convert this coordinate estimate into a bound on the stationarity measure via the time-averaging Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, which shows the time average of the l1-norms is at most one over the square root of the horizon times the coordinate sum of roots of summed squares; integrability of the gradient coordinates, of their summed squares, and of the square roots justifies integrating pointwise. This yields the stationarity measure bounded by one over the square root of the horizon times the explicit three-term expression in the gradient budget. Under the constancy hypotheses on the scalar data and with the horizon equal to n plus one, the auxiliary polynomial defining the logarithmic budget is a fixed-coefficient cubic in the horizon, so the logarithmic budget grows like the logarithm of the horizon and is eventually dominated by the square root of the horizon; expanding the gradient budget into its gap and logarithmic contributions and estimating each of the resulting summands by the corresponding rate term shows that the stationarity sequence is eventually at most a fixed constant multiple of the five-term rate, which is the asserted asymptotic domination.
nl_theorem: Consider a family, indexed by a natural number, of coordinate-wise AdaGrad settings on a differentiable objective over real d-space, driven by a stochastic gradient oracle on a probability space with a filtration, satisfying lower-boundedness, unbiasedness, coordinate-wise bounded variance, and coordinate-wise smoothness, with positive step size and stability parameter below one over the dimension. Assume the horizon of the n-th setting equals n plus one, and that the dimension, step size, stability parameter, initial suboptimality gap, the l1- and max-norms of the smoothness-constant vector and of the noise standard-deviation vector, and the max-norm of the initial gradient are all independent of n. Then there exists a real constant c at least one, independent of the family, such that the sequence of stationarity measures (the expected time average of the l1-norm of the gradient along the trajectory) is asymptotically dominated, as the index tends to infinity, by a constant multiple of the five-term rate: the initial gap over the step size times the square root of the horizon; the step size times the l1-norm of the smoothness constants times the normalised logarithmic budget over the square root of the horizon; the square root of the product of the l1-norm of the noise standard deviations and the initial gap, over the square root of the step size times the fourth root of the horizon; the square root of the product of the step size, the l1-norm of the noise standard deviations, the l1-norm of the smoothness constants, and the logarithmic budget, over the fourth root of the horizon; and the l1-norm of the noise standard deviations times the square root of the logarithmic budget over the fourth root of the horizon.

core_claim: The robust hollow star number of a hypothesis class exactly determines the smallest achievable prediction certificate size, giving a universal upper bound together with a matching worst-case lower bound.

metainfo.paper: Proofs as Explanations: Short Certificates for Reliable Predictions

nl_proof: The proof splits the conclusion into the upper bound and the matching lower bound. For the upper bound, note the hypotheses say S is itself a b-robust certificate for (x, y). By strong induction on length one extracts from S an order-preserving subsequence that is a minimal b-robust certificate, one admitting no proper subsequence that is again a certificate. Given such a minimal certificate S', prepend the heavy weighted point ((x, y'), b+1), with y' the opposite label of y, to the unit-weighted copy of S'; this weighted sequence has the correct hollow-star weight shape, is not b-robustly realizable (a low-error hypothesis would force the label y' while agreement forces y), and becomes realizable after deleting any single occurrence (deleting the heavy point leaves the realizable S', while deleting any point of S' uses minimality to expose a low-error hypothesis predicting y'). Hence it is a b-robust hollow star of length |S'|+1, so the hollow-star-number upper bound gives |S'|+1 ≤ s, i.e. |S'| ≤ s-1. For the lower bound, take a b-robust hollow star W of length s guaranteed by the attainment clause, and delete its distinguished heavy occurrence; forgetting the remaining unit weights yields a labeled sequence S_0 of length s-1. Unit-weight error identities show S_0 is b-robustly realizable and that the deleted test point lies in its b-robust agreement region, while for any proper subsequence one transfers a low-error weighted hypothesis (whose weight b+1 forces it to correctly classify the retained heavy point) through commuting erasure and sublist-monotonicity identities to conclude that the subsequence fails robust agreement, hence is not a certificate. Combining both existentials proves the theorem.
nl_theorem: Fix an input type X and a binary hypothesis class H, a set of maps from X to Boolean labels. For a corruption budget b, a finite labeled sequence is b-robustly realizable by H if some hypothesis in H disagrees with at most b of its recorded labels; a labeled test point (x, y) lies in the b-robust agreement region of a sequence S if every hypothesis in H that makes at most b errors on S predicts y at x; and S is a b-robust certificate for (x, y) when it is both b-robustly realizable and has (x, y) in its b-robust agreement region. Using nonnegative integer weights, a weighted sequence is b-robustly realizable if some hypothesis has weighted error at most b, and it is a b-robust hollow star for H if exactly one occurrence has weight b+1 and all others have weight 1, the whole weighted sequence is not b-robustly realizable, yet deleting any single occurrence makes it b-robustly realizable. The b-robust hollow star number of H is a natural number s such that every b-robust hollow star has length at most s and some b-robust hollow star has length exactly s. Assume H has b-robust hollow star number s. Then: (1) whenever a sequence S is b-robustly realizable and (x, y) lies in the b-robust agreement region of S, there is an order-preserving subsequence S' of S that is a b-robust certificate for (x, y) with length at most s-1; and (2) there exist a b-robustly realizable sequence S_0 of length exactly s-1, a test point x_0, and a label y_0 with (x_0, y_0) in the b-robust agreement region of S_0 such that no proper subsequence of S_0 is a b-robust certificate for (x_0, y_0).

core_claim: For any utility configuration instance, the algorithm's returned expected principal utility is at least the achieved approximation ratio times the optimal expected principal utility.

metainfo.paper: Polynomial-Time Approximation Schemes via Utility Alignment: Unit-Demand Pricing and More

nl_proof: Chain the packaged guarantees. Feasibility of the computed configuration gives estBoundsHold, so the estimation-to-truth guarantee yields trueBoundsHold; the objective lower-bound guarantee then gives objAlg ≤ principalAlg. The alignment guarantee gives α·principalOpt ≤ objOpt, the optimal-feasibility guarantee gives objOpt ≤ objAlg, and the returned configuration is at least as good as the computed one, so principalAlg ≤ principalReturned. Composing these four inequalities transitively delivers α·principalOpt ≤ principalReturned.
nl_theorem: Fix a fineness parameter M and alignment coefficients r, and define the achieved approximation ratio α = ((M−1)/(M+1)) · ((M−5)/(M−1) − (5/6)·(r₅/(M−1)) − (5/(M−1))·Σ_{j=6}^{M} r_j/(j−1)). A utility configuration instance packages: an integer M ≥ 6; a coefficient sequence r; a nonnegative optimal expected principal utility principalOpt; the computed configuration's expected principal utility principalAlg; the returned configuration's expected principal utility principalReturned, which is at least principalAlg; approximate-objective values objOpt and objAlg; feasibility propositions estBoundsHold (holding) and trueBoundsHold; and four guarantees, namely estBoundsHold ⇒ trueBoundsHold, trueBoundsHold ⇒ objAlg ≤ principalAlg, objOpt ≤ objAlg, and α·principalOpt ≤ objOpt. Under these hypotheses, α·principalOpt ≤ principalReturned; that is, the returned expected principal utility is at least α times the optimal expected principal utility.

core_claim: For binary-labeled data, if a bounded predictor's expected averaged two-bin calibration error does not exceed the ground-truth predictor's, then that predictor equals the ground truth almost everywhere.

metainfo.paper: A Perfectly Truthful Calibration Measure

nl_proof: Write c for the conditional expectation of the label given the first coordinate. Binary labels are integrable and lie in [0,1] almost everywhere, and since p equals c almost everywhere the same bounds hold for c. One first replaces r and c outside the binary-label event by the observed label and truncates c pointwise to [0,1]; these representatives are measurable, have residual bounded by one, and coincide almost everywhere with the original reports, so the coordinatewise almost-everywhere equalities lift through the product sample law and leave the expected errors unchanged. Applying the bias–variance formula for the expected ex-ante ATB error to each representative expresses it as 1/T times the mean squared label error plus a nonnegative threshold-averaged variance term with coefficient (T−1)/T. For the ground-truth representative, an orthogonality lemma for the conditional-expectation residual—proved via a layer-cake decomposition, a Tonelli exchange for bounded nonnegative functions, and the defining set-integral property of conditional expectation applied to each threshold indicator—shows every threshold-bin mean vanishes, killing its variance term. The corresponding term for r is nonnegative. A Pythagoras identity for the squared label error splits the mean squared error of r into the mean squared distance from c plus the label variance. Combining these, the assumed error inequality forces 1/T times the integral of the squared distance between r and c to be at most zero; since that integrand and 1/T are nonnegative, the integral is zero, so r equals c, and hence p, almost everywhere.
nl_theorem: Fix a positive integer T, a measurable space X, and a probability distribution D on pairs (x, y) with x in X and y a real number, whose label is binary in the sense that y is 0 or 1 for D-almost every pair. Let r be a measurable predictor with values in [0,1] and let p be a ground-truth predictor for D, meaning the function (x, y) ↦ p(x) agrees D-almost everywhere with the conditional expectation of the label y given the first coordinate; assume also p has values in [0,1]. Define the expected ex-ante averaged two-bin (ATB) error of a predictor as the expectation, over a sample of T independent draws from D, of the averaged two-bin calibration error of the induced report and label sequences, where the averaged two-bin error is the expectation over a uniform threshold q in [0,1] of the sum of the squares of the two bin-restricted residual sums, scaled by 1/T². If the expected ex-ante ATB error of r is at most that of p, then (x, y) ↦ r(x) agrees D-almost everywhere with (x, y) ↦ p(x). Hence the ground-truth predictor is, up to almost-everywhere equality, the unique minimizer of the expected ex-ante ATB error among [0,1]-valued measurable predictors.

core_claim: In the number-on-forehead model, if a protocol correctly decides whether the players' inputs sum to zero, then any forbidden input pattern producing one common broadcast transcript must consist entirely of identical input tuples.

metainfo.paper: Quasipolynomial bounds for the corners theorem

nl_proof: Let v be the tip of the forbidden pattern. Since every input a i shares the tip's off-diagonal coordinates, the tip's transcript agrees with the common transcript B: this is obtained by inducting on the number of rounds, peeling off the last broadcast bit and using that the next-bit rule sees only the forgotten coordinates, which coincide for v and each a i. Using validity of P, for each player i the value eval(a i) equals eval(v), because player i's guess is computed from the forgotten coordinates (equal for a i and v by the forbidden-pattern property) and from the common transcript B. It therefore suffices to show a i = v for every i. For a coordinate j different from i this is immediate from the forbidden-pattern hypothesis. For the diagonal coordinate, since eval(a i) is true the coordinates of a i sum to zero, and likewise eval(v) is true; writing the difference a i i - v i as the total sum over j of (a i j - v j), which telescopes to the difference of the two coordinate sums, this difference is zero. Hence a i = v for all i, so all the tuples a i coincide.
nl_theorem: Let G be an additive commutative group with decidable equality and let d be a positive natural number. In the d-player number-on-forehead setting each input is a tuple x indexed by the residues modulo d, and the predicate eval(x) is true exactly when the sum of the coordinates of x equals zero. A protocol P consists, for every player i, of a next-bit rule and a guess rule, each depending only on the other players' coordinates (the input with coordinate i forgotten) together with the broadcast bits produced so far; the broadcast of length t is generated by iterating the next-bit rules. Call P valid for eval after t rounds if for every input x and every player i the guess of player i, computed from the other players' coordinates and the length-t broadcast of x, equals eval(x). Let a be a family of input tuples indexed by residues modulo d that forms a forbidden pattern, meaning there is a tip tuple v with a i j = v j whenever i ≠ j. If eval(a i) is true for every i and all the tuples a i produce the same broadcast transcript B of length t, then all the tuples a i are equal.

core_claim: For any finite nonempty hypothesis class and manipulation graph, some improper randomized learner attains expected strategic regret bounded by eight times the square root of horizon times the log class size.

metainfo.paper: On Randomized Algorithms in Online Strategic Classification

nl_proof: One instantiates the Improper-Hedge learner: an exponential-weights scheme over the classifiers that mixes in the all-positive classifier for exploration, using an unbiased loss estimator supported on rounds that reveal the agent's original feature, with learning rate one half the square root of log-cardinality over horizon and exploration rate the square root of log-cardinality over horizon in the regular regime, and a zero-exploration fallback otherwise. An analysis package is constructed recording the true mixture loss, main term, Hedge, bias, and deviation terms as expectations of pathwise quantities under the interaction law. Shift invariance identifies expected strategic regret with expected shifted regret. An exploration identity decomposes shifted regret as the main term minus the exploration rate times the bounded mixture loss. In the regular regime the main term splits into Hedge, bias, and deviation contributions, bounded via a potential inequality with a conditional second-moment estimate, a conditional bias estimate, and a uniform deviation estimate obtained from an exponential-moment martingale argument and an expected-maximum lemma. Summing these bounds and substituting the parameter formulas evaluates the total to eight times the square root of horizon times log-cardinality. The degenerate cases (zero horizon, singleton class, and short horizons below log-cardinality) are handled by a crude length bound on regret together with elementary square-root arithmetic.
nl_theorem: Consider online strategic classification over a feature space with a directed manipulation graph, a fixed deterministic tie-breaking manipulation rule, and a nonempty finite family of classifiers indexed by a finite type, where the family is injective. In the interaction, at each round the learner announces a distribution over actions (either the all-positive classifier or one of the indexed classifiers), an adaptive adversary chooses a labeled example after seeing the induced distribution over classifiers, the sampled classifier is revealed, and the agent manipulates according to the rule. Then there exists an improper randomized learner such that, for every horizon T and every adaptive adversary, the expected Stackelberg regret against the best hypothesis in the class is at most eight times the square root of T multiplied by the logarithm of the class cardinality.

core_claim: In robust online decision making, the estimations-to-decisions policy's regret against any hypothesized model is at most twice the horizon times the fuzzy decision-estimation coefficient, plus the optimism bound, plus twice the horizon times the failure probability.

metainfo.paper: Regret Bounds for Robust Online Decision Making

nl_proof: First, the unit reward bound forces every robust action value and robust optimal value into [0,1], so averaged action-gaps and model-gaps stay in [-1,1]; summability of these averages comes from a Tonelli criterion for nonnegative real product families. Consequently the fuzzy decision objective, its value at a reference model, and its worst-case value all lie in [0,1]. Because the certified minimizer attains the coefficient at each reference, its one-step decision gap is bounded by the worst-case coefficient plus the corresponding loss divided by the squared radius; handling positive and zero squared radius separately and inducting over histories shows that, on the certified inaccuracy event, the cumulative decision term is at most twice the horizon times the coefficient. Adding cumulative optimism, consistency and the reward bounds keep each one-step total in [-1,1]. Reindexing histories of length T by fixed-length tuples, and using nonnegativity, summability, and normalization of trajectory weights, one proves the expected trajectory total equals T times the robust optimal value minus expected cumulative reward. A union bound over the inaccuracy and optimism certificates then bounds this expectation by the claimed right-hand side for every consistent environment. Finally, selecting an observation law from each model carrier yields a consistent environment, making the defining supremum nonempty, and taking the supremum over consistent environments gives the regret bound.
nl_theorem: Fix action and observation types together with a robust online decision framework: a reward function valued in the unit interval, a hypothesis class of robust (imprecise-probability) models, and at least one action probability mass. Let the horizon T be positive and the confidence parameter delta lie in [0,1]. Fix a nonnegative loss between robust models, a certified fuzzy decision minimizer for this framework and loss, an online estimation oracle, and functions beta and alpha of the horizon and confidence. Assume beta is an inaccuracy bound and alpha an optimism bound for this oracle, loss, minimizer, and framework. Then for every model M in the hypothesis class and every epsilon equal to the square root of beta(T,delta)/T, the regret of the estimations-to-decisions policy determined by these data—defined as the supremum, over all environments consistent with M, of T times M's robust optimal value minus the expected cumulative reward—is at most 2·T·dec^{f,L}_epsilon(hypothesis class) + alpha(T,delta) + 2·T·delta, where the coefficient is the worst-case, over reference models, of the loss-constrained fuzzy decision objective infimized over action laws.

core_claim: There exists a family of total Boolean functions whose deterministic communication complexity exceeds the per-instance complexity of jointly solving many independent copies by an unbounded additive amount, refuting the strongest direct sum conjecture.

metainfo.paper: Refuting the Direct Sum Conjecture for Total Functions in Deterministic Communication Complexity

nl_proof: The witness family is defined explicitly. For each index n one selects, from a fixed sequence of hard communication games phi_i (built with the constant parameter Q = 255·2^(10000−8)), the largest index whose game dimensions still fit inside a 2^n × 2^n matrix, and defines f_n by precomposing that game's entry function with two chosen surjections onto the coordinates {0,1}^n, packaged via choice so the total function is well defined (and set to the constant false in the degenerate regime). Given thresholds N, L, C, one picks the target index i = 178·(C+2), then n large enough (a maximum of N and the binary logarithms of the game dimensions) so that i lies in the admissible range and hence i ≤ iN(n); membership and the greatest-index property give that phi_{iN(n)} has dimensions bounded by 2^n and positive. Because precomposition with surjections preserves communication complexity and commutes with the direct sum, D(f_n) equals the matrix complexity of phi_{iN(n)} and D(f_n^l) equals that of the game's l-fold direct sum. Choosing l = 178·(L+1) ≥ L, one combines a linear lower bound D(phi_j) ≥ 10000·j (Corollary 4.24) with an upper bound D(phi_j^{178(L+1)}) ≤ 178(L+1) + j·(178·10000·(L+1) − (L+1)) (Corollary 5.8). Casting these integer bounds to the reals, abstracting the two complexities and the index as fresh nonnegative variables, and using i ≤ j together with positivity of L+1, a nonlinear arithmetic computation (nlinarith) yields D(f_n) > D(f_n^l)/l + C, completing the refutation.
nl_theorem: In the model of two-party deterministic communication complexity, where the complexity D(f) of a function f is the least depth of a binary communication protocol (with Alice and Bob alternately speaking one bit based on their own inputs) that computes f on every input, define the l-fold direct sum of a Boolean function f to be the function on l-tuples of inputs whose output is the tuple of the l per-coordinate values of f. Then there exists a family (f_n) of total Boolean functions f_n from {0,1}^n × {0,1}^n to {0,1} such that for all natural numbers N, L, and C there exist n ≥ N and l ≥ L with D(f_n) > D(f_n^l) / l + C. Equivalently, the per-instance savings of solving many copies at once grow without bound, so no additive constant C makes D(f_n^l) ≥ l·(D(f_n) − C) hold universally, refuting the strongest additive form of the direct sum conjecture.

core_claim: Under the classical character-sum estimate, the recovery procedure exactly returns the monic squarefree polynomial whose quadratic character word lies within the allowed Hamming distance of the received word.

metainfo.paper: Recovering Polynomials over Finite Fields from Noisy Character Values

nl_proof: The polynomial g itself witnesses the existential predicate defining A, so A(d, e, r) is some monic squarefree polynomial p of degree at most d whose character word is within Hamming distance e of r (the decidability instances used inside A agree with the ambient ones since decidability is a subsingleton). It then suffices to prove uniqueness: any such p equals g. Suppose p ≠ g. By the triangle inequality and symmetry of Hamming distance, the distance between the character words of p and g is at most 2e. On the other hand, one shows this distance strictly exceeds 2e, a contradiction. That minimum-distance bound is obtained as follows. First, a pointwise case analysis over the nine possible pairs of character values gives q minus the complete character sum of p·g bounded above by twice the distance between the character words plus 2d, where the number of zeros of each character word is bounded by the degree. Second, writing the product p·g as t²·f with f squarefree of degree between 1 and 2d and t of degree at most deg p, the character sum of p·g differs from that of f only where t vanishes, so it is bounded, via the Weil estimate on f, by 2d√q + d. Combining these two inequalities with the hypotheses d ≤ (ε/16)√q and e ≤ (1/8 − ε)q, and using √q ≤ q and ε ≤ 1/8, yields that twice the distance is at least (123/128)q while 4e ≤ q/2, forcing the distance to exceed 2e. This contradiction gives p = g, hence A(d, e, r) = g.
nl_theorem: Let F be a finite field whose cardinality q is odd, and let χ denote the quadratic residue character on F, sending 0 to 0, nonzero squares to 1, and nonsquares to −1. For a polynomial g over F, its character word is the function sending α to χ(g(α)), and Hamming distance counts the points where two such words differ. Define the recovery function A: given a degree bound d, an error bound e, and a received word r : F → ℤ, if there is a monic squarefree polynomial of degree at most d whose character word is within Hamming distance e of r, then A(d, e, r) is one such polynomial (chosen by choice), and otherwise it is the zero polynomial. Assume that F satisfies the Weil character-sum bound: for every squarefree polynomial h over F with degree at least 1, the absolute value of the sum over α ∈ F of χ(h(α)) is at most (deg h − 1)·√q. Let ε > 0 be real, and let natural numbers d, e satisfy d ≤ (ε/16)·√q and e ≤ (1/8 − ε)·q. Then, for every monic squarefree polynomial g of degree at most d whose character word is within Hamming distance e of r, we have A(d, e, r) = g.

core_claim: Two specific weight-six forbidden zero-one matrix patterns each admit avoiding square matrices whose number of ones grows faster than any near-linear bound predicted by the disproved conjecture.

metainfo.paper: A Refutation of the Pach-Tardos Conjecture for 0-1 Matrices

nl_proof: The claim is a conjunction, one part for each pattern, and both parts are instances of a single lower-bound principle for so-called covering patterns. A pattern is covering when it has a distinguished row with true entries at the extreme columns, together with a family of other rows equipped with left and right endpoint columns whose intervals cover every gap between consecutive columns, with each family row sharing a true entry with the distinguished row and at most one family row preceding the distinguished one. For each of S0 and S1 one exhibits such data explicitly (a distinguished row, the two-element family, and the covering intervals) and checks the covering conditions by decision procedure. The covering-pattern principle is established by combining three facts about an explicit block construction A_b indexed by a parameter b: a weight lower bound of order c0 times its side length times 2^b for an absolute positive constant c0; the fact that A_b avoids every covering pattern; and a block-diagonal interpolation argument tiling A_b across all orders n, which converts these into the stated asymptotic lower bound on the extremal function with constant C equal to one. Applying this principle to the verified covering structures of S0 and S1 yields both halves of the conjunction.
nl_theorem: Work with binary matrices, functions from a finite grid of rows and columns to the Booleans. The weight of a finite binary matrix is the number of index pairs whose entry is true. A binary matrix A contains a pattern P when there are strictly monotone maps of P's rows into A's rows and of P's columns into A's columns sending every true entry of P to a true entry of A; A is P-free when it does not contain P. For a fixed pattern P, its extremal function at n is the largest weight of any P-free n-by-n binary matrix (zero if none exists). Say a pattern P satisfies the Pach–Tardos lower bound if there exist a nonnegative real constant C and a positive integer threshold N such that, for every n at least N, the quantity n times 2 raised to the power (square root of the base-2 logarithm of n, minus C times the base-2 logarithm of the base-2 logarithm of n) is at most the extremal function of P at n. Let S0 be the 3-by-4 pattern with true entries in row 0 at columns 0 and 2, in row 1 at columns 0 and 3, and in row 2 at columns 1 and 3; and let S1 be the 3-by-4 pattern with true entries in row 0 at columns 0 and 3, in row 1 at columns 0 and 2, and in row 2 at columns 1 and 3. Then both S0 and S1 satisfy the Pach–Tardos lower bound.

core_claim: Matching enough Chebyshev moments of two distributions on an interval forces their earth-mover distance to be small, bounded by an explicit term plus the moment error.

metainfo.paper: Sharper Bounds for Chebyshev Moment Matching, with Applications

nl_proof: By the smooth Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality, the Wasserstein-1 distance equals the supremum of the pairings of p minus q against globally 1-Lipschitz, infinitely differentiable test functions. This supremum set is nonempty since it contains the pairing of the zero function, so it suffices to bound each admissible pairing by 36 divided by k plus Γ. For a fixed such test function, one distinguishes whether it satisfies the stronger analytic smoothness hypothesis: in that case the smooth Lipschitz pairing bound applies, and otherwise the master pairing bound applies. Both produce the same estimate. These bounds are obtained by approximating the test function by a damped Chebyshev (Jackson-kernel) expansion whose uniform error on the interval is controlled by the Jackson kernel's first moment, expressing the pairing with the approximant through the Chebyshev coefficients and the ordinary moment differences, and applying Cauchy–Schwarz together with the global Chebyshev-coefficient decay estimate to bound its square by Γ squared. Since every admissible pairing is thus at most 36 divided by k plus Γ, the supremum, and hence the Wasserstein-1 distance, obeys the same bound.
nl_theorem: Let p and q be probability measures on the real line whose supports lie in the interval from minus one to one. Represent the n-th Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind by evaluating Mathlib's degree-n Chebyshev polynomial, define the n-th Chebyshev moment of a measure as the integral of that polynomial against the measure, and define the squared weighted moment discrepancy of p and q up to order k as the sum over j from 1 to k of the squared difference of their j-th moments divided by j squared. Define the Wasserstein-1 distance as the infimum, over all couplings of p and q (measures on the plane with the correct first and second marginals), of the integral of the absolute difference of coordinates. Then for every positive integer k and every nonnegative real Γ, if the squared weighted moment discrepancy of p and q up to order k is at most Γ squared, the Wasserstein-1 distance between p and q is at most 36 divided by k plus Γ.

core_claim: For every tradeoff parameter and admissible approximation parameters, there is a finite domain and hypothesis class of bounded dimension for which every learning-unlearning scheme and ticketed scheme meets the stated asymptotic space lower bounds.

metainfo.paper: The Space Complexity of Learning-Unlearning Algorithms (extended abstract)

nl_proof: The witnesses are the empty domain, the empty hypothesis class, and d = 0. The empty type is finite. The Littlestone bound holds because shattering a tree of any depth would yield a hypothesis in the empty class, applying the shattering condition to the all-false branch, which is impossible, so every candidate depth is at most 0. The VC bound holds because every finite subset of the empty type is empty and has cardinality 0. The inequality 0 ≤ 1/β + 1 follows from β > 0 giving 1/β ≥ 0. Both space lower bounds hold vacuously: over the empty domain the only dataset is the empty list of length 0, so no dataset of size 1 exists; instantiating the least-upper-bound characterization of the space function at input size 1 makes space(1) − 1 an upper bound of the empty achievable set, forcing space(1) ≤ space(1) − 1, a contradiction. Hence no LU scheme and no TiLU scheme exist over the empty domain, so the statements quantified over all such schemes are satisfied trivially.
nl_theorem: Fix a real parameter β strictly between 0 and 1, a real ε in the closed interval [0,1], and a real δ in the half-open interval [0,1/2). Consider binary classification: a domain X, hypotheses X → Bool, datasets as finite lists of (point, label) pairs, and the notion that a dataset is H-realizable when some hypothesis in H matches all its labels. Define VC dimension at most d (every shattered finite subset has at most d elements) and Littlestone dimension at most d (every depth for which H shatters a complete Littlestone tree is at most d). An (ε,δ)-LU scheme for H-realizability testing is a learn/unlearn pair whose learn output's Boolean solution correctly decides realizability, whose relearn-after-removal distribution is (ε,δ)-close to relearning on the kept data, and whose space function is the least upper bound of achievable auxiliary-string lengths at each input size; a ticketed (ε,δ)-TiLU scheme is analogous but its space also accounts for per-user ticket lengths. Say a space function s obeys an Ω(g) lower bound if some positive constant c satisfies c·g(n) ≤ s(n) eventually. Then there exist a finite domain X, a hypothesis class H, and a natural number d such that the Littlestone dimension of H is at most d, the VC dimension of H is at most d, and d ≤ 1/β + 1, and moreover: every (ε,δ)-LU scheme for H-realizability testing has space obeying the lower bound Ω((1 − H(δ))·n), and every (ε,δ)-TiLU scheme has space obeying the lower bound Ω(β·(1 − H(δ))·n^(1−β)), where H(δ) is the binary entropy of δ.

core_claim: In any election, whenever a ratio condition linking the threshold and the committee size holds, some committee of bounded size is dominated by no candidate above that threshold fraction of voters.

metainfo.paper: Six Candidates Suffice to Win a Voter Majority

nl_proof: The argument builds up a fixed-point machine and turns it into a probabilistic committee-selection scheme. Arbitrarily fine barycentric subdivisions of the standard simplex are constructed and shown to contract mesh geometrically; a parity form of Sperner's lemma over such triangulations yields approximate fixed points of any continuous self-map of the simplex, and minimizing the distance between a point and its image upgrades this to an exact fixed point, giving Brouwer's theorem on the finite simplex. Applying it to the polynomial response map associated with a candidate-selection rule produces a stationary probability distribution on candidates. Ranking candidates by each voter's preference and cutting at a fractional quantile of prescribed probability mass converts the stationarity into a polynomial inequality bounding the threshold by one minus the cut mass plus its size-power. A strict integral comparison between the two sides of an admissible integral criterion, combined with the given logarithmic ratio hypothesis, rules out the possibility that every committee is dominated, forcing the existence of an undominated committee of the required size.
nl_theorem: Consider an election given by a finite voter type and a finite candidate type, where each voter has a strict total preference order over candidates. For a real threshold and a natural committee-size bound, call a candidate set undominated with that bound if it has at most that many candidates and, for every candidate, the fraction of voters who prefer that candidate to every member of the set is strictly below the threshold. Then, provided the threshold is positive and at most one, the size bound is positive, and twice the reciprocal of the size bound plus one is at most the threshold divided by one minus the natural logarithm of the threshold, there exists such an undominated committee.

core_claim: A concept class family attaining a given spherical dimension while bounding two combinatorial dimensions exists exactly when the sphere's margin classifiers admit a disambiguation respecting the same two bounds.

metainfo.paper: Spherical Dimension

nl_proof: The equivalence is proved by establishing both implications. For the forward direction, from a class witnessing the spherical-dimension side one handles n ≤ −1 by noting the integer unit sphere is empty, so the empty class disambiguates vacuously. For n ≥ 0 one extracts an antipodal simplicial m-sphere with m ≥ n whose faces are antipodally realizable, builds an equivariant, face-local vertex selector on the unit sphere in the appropriate Euclidean dimension (obtained by transporting the standard sphere through the realization homeomorphism, picking a high-barycentric-coordinate vertex on each antipodal orbit, and using uniform continuity to get a positive angular radius), restricts it to an equatorial subsphere via a linear isometry, and pulls the original class back through the selected labeled points; shattering arguments show this pullback preserves both dimension bounds while yielding a disambiguation. For the reverse direction, from a margin disambiguation one again treats n ≤ −1 directly, and for n ≥ 0 constructs a sufficiently fine antipodal triangulation of the standard sphere: starting from the cross-polytope antipodal simplicial sphere and iterating equivariant barycentric subdivision, whose realizations are preserved by an affine barycenter homeomorphism, whose face-size bound persists, and whose coordinate mesh contracts geometrically because averages over nested faces contract, giving angular diameters below ε. Choosing one representative per antipodal vertex orbit produces an equivariant labeled-point map making every face antipodally realizable by extensions of the margin classifiers centered near a face, using that ε < π/2 to secure the positive-clause priority. This exhibits admission of a simplicial n-sphere with the inherited bounds. Combining the two implications gives the biconditional.
nl_theorem: Work with binary concept classes, i.e. sets of Boolean-valued functions on a domain. Say a class has VC dimension at most an integer a if every injectively indexed finite family it shatters has cardinality at most a, and dual antipodal VC dimension at most b if every injectively indexed dually antipodally shattered subfamily has cardinality at most b (dual antipodal shattering meaning that for each labeling some domain point realizes either the labeling or its pointwise complement). Using antipodal simplicial n-spheres (finite simplicial complexes carrying a fixed-point-free involutive vertex permutation whose geometric realization is equivariantly homeomorphic to the standard unit n-sphere), say a class admits a simplicial n-sphere if there is an equivariant vertex-to-labeled-point map under which every face is antipodally realizable, and its simplicial spherical dimension is at least an integer n when n ≤ −1 or it admits a simplicial m-sphere for some natural m ≥ n. On the integer-indexed unit n-sphere, the partial angular-margin linear classifier of radius ε labels a point positively when its geodesic angle to the center is at most ε, negatively when its angle to the antipode of the center is at most ε (positive clause having priority), and leaves it undefined otherwise; a total class disambiguates such a partial class if every partial concept extends to a member agreeing wherever the partial concept is defined. The theorem states: for all integers a, b, n, there exists a domain and a binary concept class with VC dimension at most a, dual antipodal VC dimension at most b, and simplicial spherical dimension at least n, if and only if for some radius ε with 0 < ε < π/2 the partial angular-margin linear classifiers of radius ε on the n-sphere admit a disambiguating total class with VC dimension at most a and dual antipodal VC dimension at most b.

core_claim: A single polynomial-memory streaming generator family exists that, for every small-automaton target language under any surjective enumeration, eventually outputs only correct strings while omitting only polynomially many target strings.

metainfo.paper: Space-Efficient Language Generation in the Limit

nl_proof: The proof exhibits the rank-iteration generator family and combines two established properties. First, that family runs in polynomial working memory, always outputs a deterministic automaton within the state bound, and, along any surjective enumeration of a bounded target language, eventually produces an output whose symmetric difference from the target is finite. This uses a rank-refined key ordering on padded s-state candidate automata that increases strictly on rejected words but never passes the target key, forcing the candidate sequence to stabilize, together with a Boolean encoding of the finite configuration space simulating the abstract update. Second, a post-processing step restricts each output automaton to accept only words of length at least 2s−1 without altering the persistent memory. Because the finite symmetric difference cannot contain any word of length at least 2s−1 (a strict-refinement chain of finite state setoids bounds distinguishing word lengths), the restricted output becomes contained in the target, giving no hallucination, and every missed word is short. Counting words below the length cutoff yields a geometric sum bounded by C·|Σ|^(2s-2), establishing the generation-gap estimate. Feeding the three convergence properties into this post-processing yields the claimed family.
nl_theorem: Fix finite alphabets and a positive state bound s. There exists a uniform family of finite-memory streaming generators, each reading its input enumeration one alphabet symbol or word-boundary token at a time, satisfying three conditions. First, its persistent Boolean memory has at most C(s + |Σ| + 1)^d coordinates for some constants C and d, uniformly over all alphabets and bounds. Second, for every deterministic finite automaton T with at most s states over Σ and every surjection from the naturals onto L(T), there is a time after which every output language is contained in L(T). Third, for every positive s there are constants C_s and k₀ such that whenever |Σ| ≥ k₀, for each such target and enumeration there is a time after which the set of missed target words is finite and has cardinality at most C_s·|Σ|^(2s-2).

core_claim: Every affine-weighted directed acyclic graph admits a minimum shortest path cover whose size is at most a fixed absolute-constant power of vertices, dimension, and logarithm of vertices.

metainfo.paper: Shortest Paths with Linear Edge Weights

nl_proof: The witness constant is C = 12. Fix d and a graph G.
