If G has a source-to-sink path, one builds a shortest path cover by a balanced doubling construction: starting from parameter-independent one-edge minimum paths (with regions covering all of parameter space), each refinement round doubles the allowed path length by concatenating stored minimum subpaths through every intermediate vertex, subdividing each region using a bound on the number of realized affine sign patterns (at most (2m+1)^d cells for m affine comparisons, proved by induction on dimension and number of functions via a midpoint zero-crossing lemma and parametrization of nonconstant affine zero hyperplanes). After log₂ n plus one rounds every acyclic path, having no repeated vertex and thus at most n vertices, lies within the length bound, so the stored source-to-sink path on each nonempty final region is globally shortest there; collecting these yields a finite cover of size at most (2n^4+1)^(d(⌊log₂ n⌋+1)). A recurrence estimate bounds this by n^(12 d ⌊log₂ n⌋), and since a cover size is one admissible value the infimum defining the cover size is bounded accordingly; the n=1 case is handled by the unique singleton path. If G has no source-to-sink path, no shortest path cover exists (a cover would furnish one at the zero parameter), so the size is zero, which satisfies the bound.
nl_theorem: Consider directed acyclic graphs whose vertices are indexed by a finite type, whose ordered vertex pairs may carry an edge equipped with a coefficient vector giving an affine (linear plus constant) weight function of a parameter vector in d-dimensional real space, and which have distinguished source and sink vertices. For such a graph G with n vertices, define the size of its minimum shortest path cover to be the least cardinality of a set of source-to-sink paths such that, at every parameter value, some path in the set is a shortest source-to-sink path (with value zero when no such cover exists). The theorem asserts the existence of a positive absolute natural-number constant C such that for every parameter dimension d and every such graph G, the size of the minimum shortest path cover is at most n raised to the power C times d times the base-2 logarithm of n.

core_claim: Every measurable, replicable, and accurate distribution-property tester can be replaced by an equivalent one that is a random-threshold algorithm, order- and label-invariant, replicable, and permutation-robustly replicable.

metainfo.paper: On the Structure of Replicable Hypothesis Testers

nl_proof: Take A′ to be the canonicalisation of A: the random-threshold algorithm whose deterministic threshold function is the canonical score of A, obtained by first taking the seed acceptance probability of A, then averaging over all permutations of the sample positions, and finally averaging over all permutations of the domain labels. Each of the six required properties is an established property of this construction. That A′ is a random-threshold algorithm holds because its threshold is exactly the canonical score, which lies in [0,1] as an iterated average of seed acceptance probabilities lying in [0,1]. Order and label invariance follow because averaging over all position permutations, respectively all label permutations, makes the score invariant under those group actions, so the two threshold comparisons always agree. Accuracy follows from the identity that the acceptance probability of A′ under p equals the average over label permutations π of the acceptance probability of A under the relabelled distribution p^π; since symmetry keeps membership in P and farness from P under relabelling, averaging inequalities that hold for every π transfers both accuracy bounds. Replicability is obtained by converting ρ-replicability of A into a bound on the expected gap of its seed acceptance probability (score replicability), showing that both averaging steps preserve this bound via reindexing of the weighted sums, and then reconverting: for a threshold algorithm the seed disagreement probability on a pair equals the absolute gap of its threshold values. Finally, permutation-robust replicability follows because A′ is label-invariant, which lets the cross-permutation disagreement sum weighted by p^π be reindexed to the ordinary disagreement sum weighted by p, and this ordinary sum is bounded by ρ using replicability of A′.
nl_theorem: Fix a domain size n and sample size m, and encode a tester as a function A sending a sample sequence (Fin m → Fin n) and a real seed r to a Boolean decision (true = accept). Let the uniform seed measure be Lebesgue measure restricted to [0,1], and define, for each sample sequence X, the seed acceptance probability of A as the real seed measure of {r : A X r = true}; the product weight of X under a probability mass function p as the product of the values p(X i); the acceptance probability of A under p as the weighted sum of seed acceptance probabilities; and total variation distance between p and q as half the sum of |p(j) − q(j)|. Say P (a set of probability mass functions on Fin n) is symmetric if it is closed under relabelling by permutations of Fin n, and that p is ε-far from P if every q ∈ P has total variation distance at least ε from p. Suppose A is measurable (each acceptance set is Lebesgue measurable), ρ-replicable (for every p the seed-agreement probability over two independent sample sequences and one shared seed is at least 1 − ρ), and (ε,δ)-accurate for P (acceptance probability at least 1 − δ when p ∈ P, and at most δ when p is ε-far from P). Then there exists a tester A′ on the same n and m that is (ε,δ)-accurate for P, operates as a random-threshold algorithm (comparing a deterministic [0,1]-valued function of the samples against the seed), is invariant to both the order and the labels of the samples, is ρ-replicable, and is ρ-permutation-robustly replicable.

core_claim: The sign-rank of the exact k-Hamming-distance Boolean matrix on length-n binary strings is bounded by an exponential in k that does not depend on n.

metainfo.paper: Sign-Rank of k-Hamming Distance is Constant

nl_proof: The proof obtains a fixed absolute constant from a threshold-oracle-tree construction: for every n and k there is an oracle tree of depth at most two computing the exact k-Hamming-distance matrix pointwise, whose two internal queries are the Hamming-distance threshold predicates "distance at least k" and "distance at least k+1", each having support-rank at most an exponential in k. One shows the sign-rank of any oracle tree whose queries have support-rank at most r is at most (1+r²) raised to the tree depth, by inducting on the tree: leaves are constant matrices of sign-rank at most one, and at an internal query one combines sign-realizers of the two subtrees using a dominating scaled Hadamard product against the query's support matrix, whose rank is controlled by subadditivity of rank and by the fact that the rank of an entrywise product is at most the product of ranks. The support-rank bound for a threshold query comes from generic Gram matrices whose difference determinant vanishes exactly below the Hamming threshold (using a combinatorial-Nullstellensatz nonvanishing argument and a bound on the rank of block-determinant kernels). Combining the pointwise equality, congruence of sign-rank under pointwise equality, the oracle-tree bound at depth two, and elementary exponent arithmetic yields the stated uniform bound with c a concrete multiple of the base constant.
nl_theorem: Fix the following setup. A binary string of length n is a function from the finite index set of size n to the Booleans. The exact k-Hamming-distance matrix on such strings has, at position (x,y), the Boolean value that is true exactly when the Hamming distance between x and y equals k. The real sign attached to a Boolean value is -1 for false and 1 for true. A real matrix sign-realizes a Boolean matrix when the sign of each of its entries equals the prescribed real sign of the corresponding Boolean entry. The sign-rank of a Boolean matrix (with finite column index type) is the least natural number arising as the rank of a real matrix that sign-realizes it. The theorem asserts: there exists an absolute natural number c such that for all natural numbers n and k, the sign-rank of the exact k-Hamming-distance matrix on length-n binary strings is at most 2 raised to the power c·(k+1). In particular this is a uniform exponential-in-k bound that is independent of n.

core_claim: A single universal constant guarantees identity testers against a bounded distinguisher family whose sample count grows only additively beyond the given Rademacher-complexity sample parameter.

metainfo.paper: Testing Distributions Against Bounded Distinguishers

nl_proof: The result is obtained by reduction from the corresponding equivalence-testing upper bound. First one invokes the equivalence-testing theorem with the same sample parameter m and parameters ε and δ, producing a universal constant C and a measurable equivalence tester T that is correct under the promise that R_m(F,·) ≤ ε/16 for at least one of the two input distributions, with sample count bounded by m + ⌈C(1+log(1/δ))/ε²⌉. Given the reference distribution P_ref satisfying R_m(F, P_ref) ≤ ε/16, this Rademacher bound supplies the second disjunct of the equivalence promise for every unknown input distribution P paired with P_ref. The identity-from-equivalence reduction then builds an identity tester I using the same decision rule, measurability proof, and sample count as T, drawing an independent sample from the explicit reference law as its second input. Applying the equivalence tester's completeness clause with P = P_ref yields the acceptance guarantee, and applying its soundness clause when d_F(P, P_ref) > ε yields the rejection guarantee, since the identity acceptance and rejection probabilities coincide with the equivalence ones under the product law. Because the two sample counts are equal, the final sample-count inequality follows by transitivity with the same universal constant C.
nl_theorem: There exists a universal constant C > 0 with the following property. Let X be a standard Borel measurable space, let F be a countable family of measurable Boolean distinguishers on X that is closed under pointwise complementation, let m be a positive integer, let ε, δ ∈ (0,1), and let P_ref be an explicit reference probability measure. Here the fooling distance d_F(P,Q) is the supremum over f ∈ F of |E_P[f] − E_Q[f]|, and the distributional Rademacher complexity R_m(F,P) is the expected empirical Rademacher complexity of F on an m-sample from P. If R_m(F, P_ref) ≤ ε/16, then there exists a measurable (ε,δ)-identity tester T to P_ref against F, meaning: T accepts every unknown distribution equal to P_ref with probability at least 1−δ, and rejects every unknown distribution at fooling distance greater than ε from P_ref with probability at least 1−δ; moreover its sample count is at most m + ⌈C(1+log(1/δ))/ε²⌉.

core_claim: For any generalized-mean exponent at least one and any coprime population ratio exceeding one, a fast algorithm produces a fair consensus clustering within factor thirty-five of optimal.

metainfo.paper: Towards Fair Representation: Clustering and Consensus

nl_proof: The result is obtained by instantiating a generic reduction from closest-fair clustering to fair consensus at the closest-fair approximation factor 33, giving the final factor 2 + 33 = 35. The reduction builds a consensus algorithm that, for each input clustering, selects an exactly closest p/q-fair clustering (whose existence follows because the single-block clustering is fair, so the set of achievable distances to fair clusterings is nonempty and has a least element), and returns the selected candidate of minimum consensus objective. Choosing the input closest to any fair comparator and using symmetry and the triangle inequality of the disagreement distance shows each candidate's distance to every input is at most (2 + α) times the comparator's, and monotonicity plus homogeneity of real powers lifts this pointwise bound to the objective. The empty-family case returns the single-block clustering, which is fair and gives vanishing objectives. Assigning cost zero to every run trivially satisfies the quadratic time bound. The closest-fair subproblem itself is solved by the minimizing choice with cost zero.
nl_theorem: Represent a clustering of a finite type of red/blue colored points by a Boolean same-block relation, and measure the distance between two clusterings as the Hamming distance of their same-block indicators on unordered pairs, that is, the number of pairs co-clustered by exactly one of them. Call a clustering p/q-fair when every cluster's blue count times q equals its red count times p, and define the generalized-mean consensus objective of a candidate against m input clusterings as the (1/ℓ)-power of the sum of the ℓ-powers of its distances to the inputs. Then for every real ℓ ≥ 1 and coprime natural numbers p, q > 1 there exists a fair-consensus algorithm together with a natural-number cost model such that, on every finite red/blue population whose global blue-to-red ratio is p/q and which has at least as many blue points as red points, the algorithm returns a p/q-fair clustering whose consensus objective is at most 35 times that of every p/q-fair comparator, and whose cost is bounded uniformly by a constant times m² times n², where n is the number of points.

core_claim: A binary-alphabet next-token generator class is chain-of-thought learnable by every consistent rule, with sample complexity scaling in its VC dimension times the logarithm of the generation length.

metainfo.paper: A Theory of Learning with Autoregressive Chain of Thought

nl_proof: The proof extracts the universal constant from a general chain-of-thought generalization guarantee, taking c to be nine times that constant divided by log 2. One first shows that for every admissible base class, generation length, and VC bound d there is an integer D bounding the VC dimension of the 0–1 loss class of the chain-of-thought class with D ≤ (9/log 2)·d·log(2T): when d = 0 the growth function of the loss class is at most one, so its VC dimension is zero; when d ≥ 1 a Sauer-type bound for the chain-of-thought loss class yields D ≤ 3d·log₂(2T/log 2), which is converted to the desired form using 1/2 ≤ log 2 < 1 and T ≥ 1. Fixing ε and δ in (0,1), the positivity of the three logarithms log(2T), log(12/ε), log(2/δ) and the inequality 9/log 2 ≥ 1 let one bound D·log(12/ε) + log(2/δ) by (9/log 2)·(d·log(2T)·log(12/ε) + log(2/δ)). Multiplying by c₀/ε shows the real quantity required by the generalization guarantee is at most c·ε⁻¹·(d·log(2T)·log(12/ε) + log(2/δ)), whose ceiling is precisely the stated sample-complexity function. Applying the generalization guarantee with this D then yields the learnability conclusion.
nl_theorem: Work over the binary alphabet, identifying strings with finite lists of booleans. For a next-token generator f, let its apply-and-append map be x ↦ x ++ [f x], let its T-step chain-of-thought trace be the T-fold iterate of that map, and let its end-to-end map return the last token of the trace (with the empty string's last token declared to be false). Define the VC dimension of a binary function class as the supremum of the sizes of shattered finite sets, and the input part of a trace at length T by dropping its last T tokens. Say a class is chain-of-thought learnable by a consistent rule with a given sample-complexity function m(ε,δ) when, for all ε,δ ∈ (0,1), every chain-of-thought consistent rule A on m(ε,δ) traces satisfies: for every input distribution D and every target f* in the class, with probability at least 1−δ over an i.i.d. sample the induced end-to-end hypothesis has population 0–1 loss at most ε. The theorem asserts the existence of a universal constant c > 0 such that for every base class F, every positive generation length T, and every natural number d with VC(F) ≤ d, the class F is chain-of-thought learnable by every consistent rule with sample-complexity function m(ε,δ) = ⌈c·ε⁻¹·(d·log(2T)·log(12/ε) + log(2/δ))⌉.

core_claim: Clipped stochastic gradient descent under heavy-tailed noise obeys a large-deviation upper bound for its best-iterate squared gradient norm, with explicit speed and rate function in both the subthreshold and threshold regimes.

metainfo.paper: Tight Long-Term Tail Decay of (Clipped) SGD in Non-Convex Optimization

nl_proof: The proof invokes the packaged core large-deviation lemma. First, from the cost, noise, and run hypotheses one extracts an adapted bias–centered decomposition of the clipped gradient, with the bias bounded by 4σ^p γ_t^{1-p} and a conditional exponential-moment (sub-Gaussian) bound exp(3 γ_t² ‖a‖²) for the centered increment against predictable test vectors. A Lipschitz-gradient quadratic descent inequality is telescoped to bound the weighted best-iterate statistic by a deterministic schedule remainder plus a sum of inner products of predictable weights against the centered increments. A finite-horizon conditional-MGF induction turns the sub-Gaussian bounds into a Gaussian concentration estimate for that sum. Schedule asymptotics show the deterministic remainder is negligible compared with the cumulative step size and compare the concentration variance with the chosen speed, yielding a one-sided tail bound limsup (1/speed)·log μ(F_t ≥ y) ≤ −y²/C for every y ≥ 0, with C = 768 G⁴ when p < 2 and C = 384 G⁴ when p = 2. Since F_t is nonnegative, a general conversion lemma promotes these one-sided tails to the full large-deviation upper bound over arbitrary measurable sets, giving both regimes.
nl_theorem: Fix a probability space with a filtration indexed by the natural numbers, a dimension d, an objective f on d-dimensional Euclidean space, iterates x_t and stochastic gradients g_t, together with constants G, p, σ and a Lipschitz constant L. Assume the nonconvex-cost conditions (G positive, f bounded below and differentiable with gradient norm at most G and L-Lipschitz gradient), the heavy-tail noise conditions (1 < p ≤ 2, σ ≥ 0, unbiased gradients and a conditional p-th moment bounded by σ^p), and that x_t is a clipped-SGD run with the specified step size (t+2)^{-p/(3p-2)} and clipping radius. Let F_t be the best-iterate squared gradient norm min_{0≤k<t} ‖∇f(x_k)‖² (with F_0 = 0). Then: if p < 2, the sequence (F_t) satisfies the large-deviation upper bound with speed t^{4(p-1)/(3p-2)}/log t and rate function y²/(768 G⁴) for y ≥ 0 and +∞ for y < 0; and if p = 2, it satisfies the same upper bound with speed t/(log t)² and rate function y²/(384 G⁴) for y ≥ 0 and +∞ for y < 0. Here the large-deviation upper bound means the speed is eventually positive and tends to infinity, and for every measurable set B the limsup of (1/speed)·log μ(F_t ∈ B) is at most minus the infimum of the rate function over the closure of B.

core_claim: Any read-once branching program that approximately counts each symbol's frequency within a fixed additive error must have width or length large enough to satisfy a binomial inequality.

metainfo.paper: Tight Streaming Lower Bounds for Deterministic Approximate Counting

nl_proof: The proof invokes an auxiliary potential bound: from the existence of a program computing the counting problem within error Δ, one derives that binom(n+k−1, k) minus the generalized binomial coefficient Ring.choose(n − 2(k−1)Δ + k − 1, k) is at least the sum over t from 0 to n−1 of max(0, binom(t+k−1, k−1) − w). Separately, a truncated-sum lemma evaluates exactly this sum, using the maximality of m together with hockey-stick binomial identities, as binom(n+k−1, k) − binom(m+k, k) − (n−m−1)·w. Rewriting the sum in the potential inequality by this closed form and cancelling the common term binom(n+k−1, k) yields, after linear rearrangement, the stated inequality binom(m+k, k) + (n−m−1)·w ≥ Ring.choose(n − 2(k−1)Δ + k − 1, k).
nl_theorem: Fix integers k ≥ 2, n ≥ 1, w ≥ 1 and a real number Δ with 0 ≤ Δ ≤ n / (2(k−1)). A length-n width-w read-once branching program over the alphabet {1,…,k} is a layered structure with a start vertex in Fin w, a transition function sending each layer index, vertex, and read symbol to a next vertex, and an output function assigning to each terminal vertex a k-tuple of real numbers; on input x it reaches the terminal vertex obtained by iterating the transitions from the start vertex, and it computes k-counter approximate counting with error Δ if, for every input x and every symbol j, the j-th output component differs from the number of positions of x equal to j by at most Δ. Suppose such a program exists. Let m be a nonnegative integer that is at most n−1, satisfies binom(m+k−1, k−1) ≤ w, and is maximal with these two properties. Then binom(m+k, k) + (n−m−1)·w ≥ Ring.choose(n − 2(k−1)Δ + k − 1, k), where the right-hand side is the generalized binomial coefficient with real upper argument.

core_claim: For a diagonal linear recurrent network approximating a shift filter under white noise, the excess mean-square error is asymptotically a negative constant times the state-to-horizon ratio.

metainfo.paper: An uncertainty principle for Linear Recurrent Neural Networks

nl_proof: First one establishes the asymptotics of the filter energy: by expanding ‖c_k‖² as a double sum over index pairs, summing the resulting geometric series in the time index, and using that the resolvent denominator 1 − a_s conj(a_{s'}) depends only on the difference s − s', the energy equals β² times a triangularly weighted alternating sum of reciprocal denominators. Reindexing the square by the difference m = s − s' produces weights (2T+1 − |m|). A cotangent partial-fraction computation, together with the Fourier coefficients 1/(2α − iπs) of an exponential kernel, identifies the symmetric alternating series limit as 2/(e^{2α} − e^{-2α}); Cesàro averaging turns this into the limit of the triangular means. A uniform linearization bound on 1/(K·D_m) − 1/(2α − iπm), valid once the scaled frequency is at most 1/2, controls the discrepancy, yielding that the normalized triangular resolvent sum tends to 2/(e^{2α} − e^{-2α}). Combining with the exact energy identity shows the energy is asymptotically (e^{-2α}(e^{2α} − e^{-2α})/2)·S/K. Finally, expanding the white-noise loss as 1 − 2·Re(c_K) + energy, and evaluating c_K exactly (all eigenvalues collapse to e^{-α}(-1)^s at k = K, giving Re(c_K) = S·e^{-2α}(e^{2α} − e^{-2α})/(2K)), the cross term cancels one copy of the constant times S/K, leaving the excess loss asymptotic to the negated constant times S/K.
nl_theorem: Fix a real number α > 0. Define, for a state half-width T and recall horizon K, the eigenvalues a_s = exp(-α/K + iπs/K), the coefficient scale β = e^{-α}(e^{2α} - e^{-2α})/(2K), the output coefficients b_s = β·(-1)^s, and the convolution filter c_k = Σ_{s=-T}^{T} b_s · a_s^k. Let d be the shift-K filter d_k = 1_{k=K}, and let the white-noise time-domain loss be L(c,d) = Σ_{k=0}^∞ ‖c_k − d_k‖². Now take sequences T(n), K(n) of naturals with K(n) ≥ 1 for all n, with T(n) → ∞, K(n) → ∞, and (2T(n)+1)/K(n) → 0. Writing the state size S(n) = 2T(n)+1 and building c^{(n)} with parameters (α, T(n), K(n)) and d^{(n)} as the shift-K(n) filter, the excess loss L(c^{(n)}, d^{(n)}) − 1 is asymptotically equivalent, as n → ∞, to −(e^{-2α}(e^{2α} − e^{-2α})/2)·(S(n)/K(n)).

core_claim: The norm of a random vector obeys a variational high-confidence tail bound, controlled by moments of its one-dimensional marginals and a covering quantity of any aggregating measure.

metainfo.paper: Variational Tail Bounds for Norms of Random Vectors and Matrices

nl_proof: Since the seminorm is continuous on the finite-dimensional space ℝ^d and X is measurable, the map ω ↦ ‖X(ω)‖ is measurable. First establish the moment bound: for an admissible ℙ₀ and p ≥ 1, a pointwise argument shows for each fixed vector v that ‖v‖^p ≤ (∫ |⟨u, v⟩|^p dℙ₀(u)) ν(ℙ₀). Indeed, for v ≠ 0 the normalized direction x = v/‖v‖ lies on the boundary of the unit ball, so by the definition of ν the slab S = {u : |⟨u, x⟩| ≥ 1} has positive mass with 1/ℙ₀(S) ≤ ν(ℙ₀); on S we have |⟨u, v⟩| ≥ ‖v‖, and integrating gives the pointwise bound. Integrating this over ω under μ, pulling out the constant ν(ℙ₀), and swapping the order of integration by Tonelli (the integrand is jointly measurable) yields E(‖X‖^p) ≤ E₀(M_X(U,p)) ν(ℙ₀). Next fix an admissible ℙ₀ and exponent p ≥ 1 and set C = e^{t/p}(E₀(M_X(U,p)))^{1/p}ν(ℙ₀)^{1/p}, so that C^p = e^t · E₀(M_X(U,p))ν(ℙ₀). Treating the cases where the right-hand moment product is infinite, zero, or strictly positive and finite—the last via Markov's inequality applied to ‖X‖^p together with the moment bound—shows the complement {‖X‖ > C} has measure at most e^{-t}, so {‖X‖ ≤ C} has measure at least 1 - e^{-t}. Finally, letting V be the set of all such thresholds C as ℙ₀ ranges over admissible measures and p over [1, ∞), the optimized value Φ(t) equals the infimum of V. Choosing an antitone sequence in V tending to inf V and using continuity of measure from below, the lower bound 1 - e^{-t} survives passage to the infimum threshold, giving μ{ω : ‖X(ω)‖ ≤ Φ(t)} ≥ 1 - e^{-t}.
nl_theorem: Let d be a natural number and let (Ω, μ) be a probability space. Let ‖·‖ be a seminorm on the Euclidean space ℝ^d, and let X : Ω → ℝ^d be a measurable random vector. For a probability measure ℙ₀ on ℝ^d with U ∼ ℙ₀ and a real exponent p ≥ 1, write the marginal moment M_X(u,p) = E(|⟨u, X⟩|^p) (integrating over X), the aggregated moment E₀(M_X(U,p)) = ∫ M_X(u,p) dℙ₀(u), and the covering quantity ν(ℙ₀) = sup over x on the boundary of the unit ball {y : ‖y‖ ≤ 1} of 1 / ℙ₀(|⟨U, x⟩| ≥ 1), all valued in [0, ∞]. Call ℙ₀ admissible when ν(ℙ₀) < ∞. Define the optimized tail-bound value Φ(t) as the joint infimum, over all admissible probability measures ℙ₀ and all real exponents p ≥ 1, of e^{t/p} (E₀(M_X(U,p)))^{1/p} ν(ℙ₀)^{1/p}. Then for every t ≥ 0, with probability at least 1 - e^{-t} one has ‖X‖ ≤ Φ(t); that is, the event {ω : ‖X(ω)‖ ≤ Φ(t)} has μ-measure at least 1 - e^{-t}.

core_claim: The best online learner's worst-case cumulative prediction loss for smooth functions is bounded, up to a constant, by the reciprocal of the smaller smoothness parameter.

metainfo.paper: Worst-case Error Bounds for Online Learning of Smooth Functions

nl_proof: The proof assembles two comparison estimates and one diagonal bound. First, along the diagonal, the nearest-neighbor learner, which predicts the observed value at a closest previously queried point, is analyzed: its cumulative loss equals a sum over insertion edges of powered endpoint differences of the target. A pointwise crossing-weight argument, using that successive left-to-right and right-to-left crossing edges through any point halve in length, bounds the summed local action by 4/η; combined with a local Hölder estimate derived from absolute continuity and Hölder's inequality, this yields that the optimal (1+η)-power loss on F_{1+η} is O(η^{-1}). Second, when ε ≤ δ, clipping a learner's prediction to a unit interval around the last observed value, which is valid because functions in the class oscillate by at most one, converts (1+ε)-power errors into (1+δ)-power errors at cost of a factor two, giving opt_{1+δ}(F_{1+ε}) ≤ 2·opt_{1+ε}(F_{1+ε}). Third, when δ ≤ ε, monotonicity of L^p norms on the probability space (0,1] shows F_{1+ε} ⊆ F_{1+δ}, giving opt_{1+δ}(F_{1+ε}) ≤ opt_{1+δ}(F_{1+δ}). Selecting the case according to which parameter is the minimum reduces the two-parameter claim to the diagonal bound at min(δ,ε), and the constant 2C works uniformly, which is exactly the required eventual upper-order estimate along the two-parameter limiting filter.
nl_theorem: Consider online learning of real functions on the unit interval. On each trial the learner is queried at a point in [0,1], outputs a prediction, and then the true function value is revealed. For a real exponent p and a class F of functions, define the cumulative loss of a learner along a finite query sequence as the sum of the p-th powers of the absolute prediction errors, with the first query used only to initialize the learner without incurring loss; the worst-case loss of a learner over F is the supremum of this cumulative loss over all functions in F and all finite query sequences contained in [0,1]; and the optimal loss opt_p(F) is the infimum of the worst-case loss over all deterministic learners. For q ≥ 1 let F_q be the class of functions that are absolutely continuous on [0,1], whose q-th power of the absolute derivative is integrable there, and whose integral of that q-th power over [0,1] is at most 1. Then, considering pairs (δ, ε) in (0,1)×(0,1), the quantity opt_{1+δ}(F_{1+ε}) is of upper order O(min(δ,ε)^{-1}) as min(δ,ε) tends to zero: there is a finite nonnegative constant C such that, eventually for such pairs whose minimum is small enough (with either coordinate allowed to remain bounded away from zero), opt_{1+δ}(F_{1+ε}) is at most C times the reciprocal of min(δ,ε).

core_claim: The average treatment effect can be recovered from censored observational data across all realizable studies exactly when the concept classes meet a specific identifiability condition.

metainfo.paper: What Makes Treatment Effects Identifiable? Characterizations and Estimators Beyond Unconfoundedness (Extended Abstract)

nl_proof: The equivalence splits into necessity and sufficiency. For necessity, suppose a fixed map f recovers the effect from every realizable study's censored distribution. Given two same-arm compatible tuples whose expectations differ, whose covariate marginals agree, and whose reweighted measures agree, one replaces the given propensities by the induced ones inside the reweighted measures using the almost-everywhere agreement, deduces that the two witnessing studies share the same law of (X, T) (via measure-level rectangle arguments in each arm), then glues the unchanged and selected potential-outcome arms over this common treatment marginal into a new realizable study. A decomposition of the censored distribution by treatment arm shows this new study shares its censored distribution with one witness, so f forces equal effects; the marginal decomposition of the effect then contradicts the assumed inequality of expectations, establishing the condition. For sufficiency, define f on a censored distribution as the effect of any realizable representative (and zero otherwise); well-definedness follows because two realizable studies with equal censored distributions have equal arm covariate marginals and equal reweighted outcome measures, so the identifiability condition, applied to the two directly compatible arm tuples, excludes its second and third clauses and yields equal arm expectations, whence the marginal decomposition gives equal effects. Combining the two directions gives the biconditional.
nl_theorem: Model an observational study in covariate dimension d as a probability measure on complete outcomes (X, T, Y(0), Y(1)), where X ranges over d-tuples of reals, the treatment T is Boolean, and both potential outcomes are real. The censored distribution is the pushforward of the study's law along the map that reveals only the treated outcome, giving the law of (X, T, Y(T)); the average treatment effect is the integral of Y(1) − Y(0); the induced propensity score for arm t is the regular conditional probability of T = t given (X, Y(t)); and the outcome marginal for arm t is the joint law of (X, Y(t)). A study is realizable with respect to concept classes (P, H) when both induced propensity scores lie in P, both outcome marginals lie in H, and both marginals have finite first moment in the outcome coordinate. A tuple (p, P) is compatible in arm t if p ∈ P, P ∈ H, and some realizable study has arm-t outcome marginal P and arm-t propensity equal to p almost everywhere with respect to P. The concept classes satisfy the identifiability condition if, for each arm and every two same-arm compatible tuples (p, P) and (q, Q), at least one holds: their outcome expectations coincide, their covariate marginals differ, or the propensity-reweighted measures differ. Then the average treatment effect is identifiable from the censored distribution across all realizable studies (there is one fixed map from censored distributions to reals that returns each study's effect) if and only if (P, H) satisfy the identifiability condition.
